There are at least three ways to look at this:

a) GAME. Their actions were ultra vires as the game provides no
mechanics for such negotiation. Rob's action was like asking your
father what cards he was holding. Without a card effect such as
Tortured Confession or Monocle of Clarity, such talk is just empty
noise.

b) LAW. I am not sure if there are any relevant UK statutes but I
believe that there are two relevant principles of common law:

i) For a contract to exist, both parties must receive something. Rob
wanted immunity from the bloodhunt. It's not clear what consideration
your father was to receive in return. Arguably, Rob was asking your
father for his opinion on how he would behave. Because he was not
paying for this opinion and because your father had no duty of care to
Rob, Rob had no recourse when the opinion proved to be wrong.

ii) Gaming contracts are not enforceable in law. This is because
gaming is frivolous and addictive and so is against the public
interest. And, of course, "de minimus non curat lex" (the law does
not concern itself with trifles).

c) MORALITY. In these secular days, this is mostly a matter of
personal preference. In this context, the game encourages one to
follow the morality of the blood-sucking fiends that one is
role-playing. Which clan was your father playing? How honourable are
they? How highly do they prize the Eye of Hazimel? Absent such
special factors, I'd say that Rob's vampire committed the vile act of
diablerie, suffered the traditional sanction of vampire society and
that this was entirely proper. Should his cries of "entrapment" have
been considered a mitigating circumstance and grounds for mercy? I
doubt it. He still should have known better.

Andrew

If by OK you mean legal, sure. But I don't think it's *smart* to break
deals. I think that having a reputation for sticking by your word lets
you cut more and better deals, resulting in more game wins despite the
times when keeping your word hurts you.

Add to that the pride of being honest and fair-dealing, and take into
account that breaking your word is more likely to hurt feelings or
anger others than keeping it. I suggest always keeping deals.

I also suggest having a precise memory of the times your Dad has
broken deals, and reminding others of those times loudly whenever he's
trying to make a deal that will hurt you. And if keeping a deal ever
screws you up, cite that as an example of your trustworthiness if
anyone ever balks at making a deal with you.

Keeping your word doesn't mean you can't be ruthless, after all. :)

I'm appalled. Certainly, this must be a joke. Allow me a moment to defend my
honor. I figure I've played in about 60 tournaments and, as can be attested to
by all, have never broken a deal.

The game in question. GenCon North Amer. Championships, round 2. As part of
some arrangement, I gave Mr. Halcyan, my current prey, 3 turns with me leaving
him alone. After the first turn my predator played a 1st Tradition, after my
second turn, my predator played *two more* 1st Traditions. At this point, I
could have left Mr. Halcyan alone and skipped my turn but it wouldn't have
mattered. At best he would have been able to take one more turn. His prey had
plenty of pool and there's no way he could have obtained a VP if I had let him
live. I explained all of this to him and he seemed to be on board with what was
about to happen. Either Darby was about to kill us both or I would take Halcyan
out and maybe have a slim chance at keeping Darby at bay. I only proceeded
because I thought we were of the same mind. I'm willing to chalk this up as an
unfortunate misunderstanding. Maybe I'll have a chance to make it up to you in
the future. :)
